title: Your doing is sweet
hook: tera keeaa meethaa laagai: what You do seems sweet to me (Asa M5, ang 394)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lord stood up to finish the saints' work at the pool. Your line was he finished it.

Tera keeaa meethaa laagai. Four words in Punjabi, short enough to say in a single breath, before a meeting or at a hospital door. In Raga Asa, on Ang three hundred ninety-four, Guru Arjan says them plainly: what You do seems sweet to me. Hear it once and it sounds gentle. Hear it on a hard day and it sounds almost impossible. That gap between the gentle and the impossible is where today's line lives.
screen: `TERA KEEAA MEETHAA LAAGAI.` → `ASA, ANG 394.` → `GENTLE, OR IMPOSSIBLE?`

segments.voice: Back on day sixty-four, tradition placed these words in Lahore; today, the line itself. Here's the couplet, paraphrased: what You do seems sweet to me; Nanak asks for the treasure of the Lord's Name. Take the words one at a time. Tera, yours. Keeaa, the doing. Meethaa, sweet. Laagai, it seems, it strikes me as. Notice that last word. The Guru doesn't say everything that happens is pleasant. He says how it lands on him. Sweetness here is a way of receiving, not a weather report. And notice the second half. The request isn't for a better outcome. It's for the Name: not change what's happening, but give me the treasure that lets me meet it. That's the heart of what Sikhs call bhana, the Lord's will, and accepting it. It's easy to mishear. Accepting the will isn't shrugging at injustice; Sikh teaching also speaks of standing up to wrong. It's more like a settled place inside, from which a person can act without bitterness. Sikh tradition recalls this line alongside Guru Arjan's last days in Lahore, when, tradition says, he was tortured and killed under the Mughal authorities, and met that suffering steadily, remembering the One. And accepting the will never means accepting harm: if someone is hurting you, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `TERA, KEEAA, MEETHAA, LAAGAI.` · `HOW IT LANDS, NOT THE WEATHER.` · `ASKING FOR THE NAME, NOT AN OUTCOME.` · `BHANA: ACCEPTING THE WILL.` · then, large: `YOUR WILL IS SWEET.`

segments.voice: Choose something small that didn't go your way this week, a delay, a plan that changed, and let it be what it is for a moment without arguing. On the in-breath, tera keeaa; on the out-breath, meethaa laagai. If the sweetness doesn't come, that's all right; just notice the place inside where it might, and if you pray, ask for the Name, as the line does.
Your doing is sweet. Tera keeaa meethaa laagai: what You do seems sweet to me, and Nanak asks for the treasure of the Name. Today's word.
Your line: your will is sweet. Four words, and a request for the Name. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Tera keeaa meethaa laagai is sung in kirtan and repeated by Sikhs as a short line of acceptance; it is often recalled in remembrance of Guru Arjan's martyrdom.
